transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-08-17
Time: 11:00 AM PST
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kumar (Redwood SE), Alex Gomez (Redwood SRE), Mark Benson (Skyline CTO), Leah Ortiz (Skyline ML Eng), Samir Patel (Skyline Platform Eng), Ruth Chen (Skyline Security)

Summary: quick sync on latency numbers, TTFT spike between runs, plan for streaming tests and kernel tuning

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — review last week's runs, TTFT anomalies, streaming tests, kernel choices and next steps.
[00:18] Mark Benson: yep thanks. we saw the p50 okay but TTFT moved up about 80 to 120ms on the latest snapshot, which is worrying for our user flows.
[00:32] Priya Kumar: i looked at the traces, and there's a clear pre-token setup time bump. could be model load, cold kv-cache, or pipeline scheduling — would like to isolate streaming behavior first.
[00:46] Leah Ortiz: to add, our typical seq len is 128 but we have tails at 512 for some internal reports, so we're sensitive to both ttft and p95.
[01:02] Samir Patel: also want to note we reproduce locally with our 2xA10 staging cluster but the numbers are slightly better than in your hosted feed — maybe config mismatch.
[01:18] Priya Kumar: possible. two things: streaming mode reduces TTFT because token generation starts as soon as first token is available, but it introduces more small RPCs and slightly higher overhead on the infra side. non-streaming batches can give better overall throughput but worse TTFT.
[01:37] Jordan Lee: quick clarification — when you say streaming do you mean Redwood's chunked streaming with prefix KV cache warmup, right?
[01:44] Priya Kumar: yes, exactly. the streaming we tested does early-first-token emission while continuing backend decoding; we've seen ~100-180ms TTFT reductions on similar workloads using streaming.
[02:02] Mark Benson: in last run we toggled streaming on and saw inconsistent results. sometimes it helped, sometimes it didn't — maybe due to sequence length distribution or kernel fallback.
[02:16] Alex Gomez: i pulled the kernel logs — there were a few fallbacks to the slower triton kernel for -- uh, the quantized path when the sequence exceeded 256, which explains spikes at the p95. we need to confirm kernel selection thresholds.
[02:33] Ruth Chen: from a security perspective, we also need to ensure any dedicated pool or private deployment keeps audit logs and KMS usage visible. we'll need sample logs and key rotation policy.
[02:47] Jordan Lee: noted, we'll include sample audit logs. Priya, can you walk through the perf numbers you generated?
[02:54] Priya Kumar: sure — i ran three configs: hosted small batch, hosted streaming combined, and dedicated reserved GPUs. For seq len 128: hosted non-streaming p50 ~ 210ms TTFT, streaming p50 ~ 115ms TTFT. p95 moved from ~420ms to ~310ms. For seq len 256: we saw p50 go from 260ms to 160ms with streaming but occasional spikes to 700ms when kernel fallback happened.
[03:34] Leah Ortiz: that kernel fallback is our main worry — do you know why it happened?
[03:39] Priya Kumar: two hypotheses: 1) quantized model path hits a dequant code-path for >256 tokens and selects a more conservative kernel; 2) internal allocator fragmentation caused slow path. logs show 'kernel_selection: fallback->triton-simple-quant' a few times.
[03:57] Alex Gomez: i can add to that — our runtime chooses kernels based on seq length, batch size and available memory. if KV cache can't be in VRAM we spill to host which triggers the slower kernel. Samir, any chance your staging has tighter memory headroom?
[04:14] Samir Patel: possible; our docker limits were tightened last week. i'll relax them for the next test.
[04:20] Jordan Lee: good. action item — Samir to relax staging memory limits and re-run single-shot reproducer.
[04:27] Mark Benson: going back to streaming vs non-streaming: operationally, we prefer streaming because that optimizes customer-perceived latency, but only if p95 is reasonable. we can't have those 700ms outliers.
[04:41] Priya Kumar: agreed. two tuning knobs to attack outliers: 1) enforce kernel pinning to the fast kernel for up to 512 if memory allows; 2) use aggressive KV cache pre-warm for frequent prefixes so first requests see warm cache.
[04:58] Jordan Lee: can you explain kernel pinning?
[05:01] Priya Kumar: yes, kernel pinning is a runtime hint to prefer the optimized cuda/cutlass/flash-attn path instead of falling back. it increases VRAM usage slightly but keeps latency bounded. we can test with a pinned fast kernel config.
[05:17] Leah Ortiz: what's the impact on cost? if VRAM goes up we may need larger instances which affects unit economics.
[05:24] Priya Kumar: correct. for our bench, moving from A10 to A100 for pinned kernel reduced p95 by ~200ms but increased cost per token by ~30%. there's a tradeoff. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching configs to compensate.
[05:40] Mark Benson: do you have recommended batch sizes for our workload? our concurrent QPS target is ~60 rps, avg tokens 80.
[05:49] Priya Kumar: for 60 rps and token 80, continuous batching with micro-batches of 4-8 and a max batch latency of 12ms gave best results in previous pilots. But that assumes predictable arrival patterns; bursty traffic needs larger headroom.
[06:06] Alex Gomez: also consider grouping by seq len — similar-length grouping avoids wasting compute. our runtime supports length-aware routing.
[06:15] Samir Patel: what about TTFT for cold starts — do warm pools solve that?
[06:19] Priya Kumar: yes, dedicated pools with kept-warm workers reduce cold TTFT substantially. We also have hot-warm configurations: keep a small warm fraction and spin up cold instances on demand.
[06:31] Mark Benson: we are interested in dedicated reserved capacity if it gives stable p95 under our SLOs. what's the SLA on TTFT?
[06:38] Jordan Lee: dedicated has SLA on availability and predictable throughput; we can target lower jitter. We'll propose a dedicated pool with autoscale policies tuned to your load.
[06:47] Leah Ortiz: one more question: how does streaming affect token billing? are we billed earlier tokens differently?
[06:53] Jordan Lee: billing is per token generated — streaming doesn't change token count, it only changes when tokens are emitted. cost-wise same, but there may be slight network overhead costs.
[07:05] Priya Kumar: i want to call out a detail — our earlier p95 spikes happened when we crossed seq len 256 and quantized kernels fell back. i recommend we run a matrix: seq len 128/256/512 x streaming on/off x kernel pinned/unpinned. that will tell us the sweet spot.
[07:24] Mark Benson: yes please. can you also capture the TTFT breakdown — OS scheduling, kernel launch, model load, kv warmup? those waterfall traces were very helpful last time.
[07:35] Priya Kumar: will do. i'll include flame traces and tracer logs.
[07:40] Ruth Chen: security asks — we'd like a sample of audit logs (redacted) showing request ids, timestamps, and key id usage. also SSO metadata: SAML cert and redirect endpoints.
[07:52] Jordan Lee: we can provide redacted logs and SSO metadata. We'll also include KMS rotation docs.
[07:58] Samir Patel: one more ops nit — in staging we saw a few OOM messages during stress tests. Alex, do you have those logs?
[08:06] Alex Gomez: yes, i captured them. looks like when multiple long-seq requests hit simultaneously, allocator fragmentation caused an OOM and then kernel fallback. we can mitigate with larger slab allocators.
[08:21] Priya Kumar: for the next run i'll enable a larger allocation pool and run with pinned kernels. we'll also measure memory overhead so we can advise on instance type.
[08:32] Jordan Lee: perfect. timelines? Priya you mentioned by 8/20 for the streaming runs. Alex will have the dedicated cluster by 8/24. Jordan will share the spreadsheet by 8/19.
[08:42] Mark Benson: sounds good. one last thing — can we run a user-facing perf test: i.e., real frontend simulated calls to measure end-to-end latency (network included)?
[08:51] Priya Kumar: yes, we recommend including the frontend clients in the load test. Redwood can provide a small runner for that or you can reuse your synthetic harness.
[08:59] Leah Ortiz: ok we'll plan to include that.
[09:03] Jordan Lee: great. i'll recap next steps at the end and post the links: benchmark sheet, perf traces, runbook excerpt, security docs.
[09:12] [--- 20 minutes of detailed kernel logs and run commentary redacted for brevity ---]
[29:15] Priya Kumar: quick note from the kernel logs — 'flash-attn' path used successfully for 98% of requests under pinned mode, fallback only when memory headroom < 6%.
[29:30] Samir Patel: ok that suggests we need at least 6% extra VRAM headroom. we'll adjust instance sizes.
[29:38] Mark Benson: can you tell us expected cost delta for that headroom?
[29:42] Priya Kumar: rough estimate: bumping instance class to next tier increases hourly cost ~25-35% but reduces p95 by ~150-220ms; we'll quantify in the spreadsheet.
[29:55] Ruth Chen: from compliance side, if we move to dedicated, we need to ensure chain-of-custody for keys and a retention policy for logs. we'll share the policy doc.
[30:07] Jordan Lee: understood. we'll provide the log retention options and KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM options).
[30:17] Alex Gomez: also recommend enabling prefix KV caching for common prompts to lower hot-path latency. That gave a 30-50ms improvement in previous customers.
[30:28] Leah Ortiz: can you show us example config?
[30:31] Priya Kumar: yes, i'll attach a sample config in the spreadsheet.
[30:36] Mark Benson: ok final recap please.
[30:38] Jordan Lee: recap — Priya runs matrix tests (seq len 128/256/512 x streaming on/off x pinned kernels) and shares results by 8/20. Jordan shares benchmark sheet + traces by 8/19. Alex to provision dedicated cluster for final stress test by 8/24. Ruth to confirm security signoffs by 8/21. We'll meet next week to review the numbers and decide on dedicated commit.
[30:58] Priya Kumar: small note — i'll include both TTFT breakdown and memory profiles.
[31:04] Mark Benson: thanks all, appreciate the quick turn.
[31:08] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links.

References shared: benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.s3.amazonaws.com/skyline/benchmarks/2027-08-17.csv), kernel logs (link: internal: /runs/skyline/2027-08-17/kernellogs.tar.gz), security checklist (link: https://redwood.docs/security/skyline-scc.pdf)

End of transcript.
